content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all four blind responses the settled consensus is that a 'name' in Scripture symbolizes the essential character, identity, authority, and revealed nature of its bearer — supremely God's or Jesus' name, which stands for the person himself, his presence, reputation, and power. Complementary facets include delegated authority ('in the name of'), reputation/renown, covenant ownership, new-name identity, and a minority 'Name theology' in which God's name dwells in the sanctuary as a mode of presence (Deut 12:5; 1 Kgs 8).","book_summary":"The book defines the Name as the covenant identity of a house, constituted by three specific components: the Head's Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood (mirroring the ark's contents — manna, tables of the covenant, Aaron's budded rod, Heb 9:4). Substituting any component produces a counterfeit Name; rejecting, replacing, or removing any component is what it means to take the Name in vain (Ex 20:7). The book explicitly flags the common teaching ('character, authority, and reputation') as the view it is moving beyond.","consensus_core_identification":"Name = the identity/character/authority of the person who bears it; God's name = God himself as revealed, present, and powerful.","book_core_identification":"Name = the covenant identity of a house, structurally composed of Word + covenant law + priesthood; misuse of the Name = tampering with any of these three constituents.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book keeps 'identity' as the operative category (and overlaps with the consensus's 'Name theology' alternative, where God's name dwells in a house), but it narrows and structuralizes that identity into exactly three covenant components attached to a house rather than diffuse personal attributes. It reclassifies key cases: Exodus 20:7 ('take the name in vain') shifts from misuse of the divine name in speech/oath to rejecting/replacing/removing Word, law, or priesthood; Isaiah 4:1 becomes an image of claiming the Name while supplying one's own 'bread and apparel' (a counterfeit). It also introduces a 'counterfeit Name' category absent from the consensus, and excludes readings where the name is simply personal reputation or a spoken label.","material_contradiction":"None strictly. The book does not deny that the Name expresses the Head's character and authority; it specifies the covenantal-structural form that identity takes. A house bearing its Head's Word, law, and priesthood is a compatible (if idiosyncratic) elaboration of 'name = identity,' and dovetails with the consensus's own Deuteronomistic 'name dwells in the house' alternative (2 Sam 7:13; 1 Kgs 8:20).","rationale":"The central referent — name as identity, and God's Name as associated with his covenant presence in a house — survives in the book, so this is not DIVERGENT. But the book materially changes precision and boundary: it fixes the content of that identity as a three-part covenant structure keyed to the ark's contents, redefines 'in vain' as structural substitution rather than verbal misuse, and adds the counterfeit-Name concept. That is real boundary disagreement (case reclassification) within a preserved category, i.e., REFINED. It is not NOVEL because 'identity' and 'name dwelling in the temple/house' both appear in the blind consensus.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"Against REFINED, one could argue DIVERGENT: the consensus identifies the Name with a person (God/Christ himself), while the book identifies it with an institutional structure of a house, and its reinterpretation of Exodus 20:7 effectively replaces the standard referent of 'taking the name in vain.' The citation chain (ark 'called by the name' → ark contents = Word/law/priesthood → therefore Name = those three things) is inferential and never stated in the excerpts, so one could also judge the printed support insufficient rather than partial.","confidence":"medium"}
